questions.q: In Waterfall, what has to happen before the Design phase begins?
options: The Requirements phase must be complete and signed off
Nothing — Design and Requirements run at the same time
The system must already be built and tested
A sprint retrospective
questions.explain: Waterfall moves through phases once, in strict order — requirements finish and are signed off before design starts, and so on down the chain.

questions.q: What does an Agile team do differently from a Waterfall team when it comes to requirements?
options: It keeps revisiting and adjusting requirements every short cycle based on feedback
It gathers all requirements once, up front, and never revisits them
It skips requirements entirely and builds whatever developers prefer
It outsources requirements gathering to a separate department
questions.explain: Agile breaks work into short, repeating cycles — plan, build, review, adapt — so requirements keep evolving as the team and stakeholders see the product take shape.

questions.q: Why does Waterfall fit a regulatory report with a legally defined format better than it fits a new internal dashboard?
options: Because the report's requirements are genuinely stable and well understood up front, while a dashboard's requirements often shift once business users see it
Because regulatory reports never need testing
Because dashboards cannot be built using any phased approach
Because Waterfall is always faster than Agile regardless of the work
questions.explain: Waterfall's rigidity is a good fit exactly when requirements won't change mid-project — a legally defined report format is stable; a dashboard's requirements usually shift as stakeholders react to seeing it.

questions.q: In a hybrid approach, what typically stays Waterfall-style while the actual build runs in Agile sprints?
options: The up-front charter/budget and the final formal sign-off
Every individual code commit
The daily stand-up meeting
The choice of programming language
questions.explain: A common hybrid keeps Waterfall's up-front charter and final sign-off for budgeting and executive buy-in, while running the actual build work in short Agile sprints in between.

questions.q: A manager says, 'The charter is approved, let's get it into the backlog for sprint planning.' What does this sentence tell you about how this team works?
options: The team is using a hybrid approach, mixing Waterfall vocabulary (charter) with Agile vocabulary (backlog, sprint)
The team has abandoned Agile entirely
The team has abandoned Waterfall entirely
The sentence is a contradiction and doesn't reflect how any real team works
questions.explain: "Charter" is Waterfall vocabulary (an up-front, signed-off scope) while "backlog" and "sprint planning" are Agile vocabulary — hearing both in one sentence is a strong signal of a hybrid shop, which is how most real companies actually operate.
